title: Split the money, keep the average
hook: Does spreading money across bets cost you returns? Or just risk?

knows: expected value: the average result over many tries
that two coin flips can land four ways
doesNotKnow: that splitting across independent bets cuts the chance of the worst outcomes without changing the average
that this depends on the bets being independent

misconception: Splitting your money must lower what you expect to make.
objective: The learner can explain that splitting money across independent bets leaves the average unchanged while making extreme outcomes rarer, because the bets partly cancel, and that this needs independence.

claims.text: On the stage now, two bets: you lose only if both fall: ½ × ½ = 25% (split equally across two independent bets that each pay +20% or −10% with equal chance, the loss is −10%).
claims.source: Four equally likely cases: both up +20%, one each (2 cases) (20 − 10)/2 = +5%, both down −10%. P(loss) = 1/4. | REVISED v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): At the reveal the stage now pins the 2-bet chart (chip: 'Showing 2 bets, as the answer explains'), so the 25% and +5% the reveal explains are on screen even if the learner's slider passed 2 quickly (r5: 1 → 3 unlocked the reveal without the 2-bet state in view). Numbers unchanged.

claims.text: Half the time one bet rises and one falls, for +5%.
The average stays +5% however many bets the money is split across.
claims.source: Each bet's expected return is 0.5 × 20 + 0.5 × (−10) = 5; an equal split's expected return is the average of the bets' expected returns, 5, for every n. Demo.tsx average(n) enumerates the binomial outcomes.

claims.text: The worst case, every bet falling (−10%), has chance 50%, 25%, 12.5%… halving with each added bet.
The chance of some loss does not fall at every step: with 4 bets it is 31.3%, more than the 25% with 2.
The lesson is a model: truly independent bets with made-up numbers; real investments often fall together, and it is not advice.
claims.source: Diversification reduces risk only to the extent assets are not perfectly correlated; market-wide (systematic) risk cannot be diversified away (Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 27). Shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

claims.text: As you split across more bets, the chance of some loss does not fall at every step, but the worst case, every bet falling, gets rarer at every step.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 3. Exact check (bets.mjs): average loss when there is a loss is -10.0% for 1, 2 and 3 bets (the only losing outcome is the worst case), then -4.0%, -5.0%, -5.7% for 4, 5, 6 bets. So the second half is true from 4 bets on, but not at 2 or 3 bets, where every loss is the full -10%. The sentence is also silent on 'small compared with what'. Consider 'and the big loss gets rarer' or restricting to 4+ bets. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: node: exact loss chance 50, 25, 12.5, 31.25, 18.75, 10.94% for n=1..6; the average loss when there is a loss is -10% for n=1,2,3 and only -4.0, -5.0, -5.7% for n=4,5,6. So 'the losses left are small ones' is false at 2-3 bets (the loss is the full -10%) and 'small' is unanchored. Fix: restrict to 4+ bets or say 'and the big loss gets rarer: 50%, 25%, 12.5%'. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was '... but the losses left are small ones' (disputed: at 2-3 bets the loss is the full -10%; 'small' unanchored). Worst-case chance is 0.5^n, true at every step. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-derived in node: loss chance 50, 25, 12.5, 31.25, 18.75, 10.94% for n=1..6 (not monotone); worst case 0.5^n halves each step. Matches reveal.

claims.text: Chart labels: the 0% bar is labelled 'break even'; every bar has a return tick under it (e.g. −10%, 0%, +10%, +20% at 3 bets).
claims.source: outcomes(n) in Demo.tsx: returns (k × 20 + (n − k) × (−10)) / n for k = 0..n; at n = 3 these are −10, 0, +10, +20. A 0% result is neither gain nor loss (lossChance counts r < 0 only). | REVISED v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. New stage text (r5 minor).

recall.question: You split money equally between two independent bets with the same average return. Compared with putting it all in one, what changes?
options: The average stays the same; the worst outcome gets rarer
recall.why: Each bet has the same average, so the split does too. Both have to go badly for the worst case, which is less likely than one going badly.
